title: They Rode This Bridge for Fun. Then It Fell.
alt_titles: The Bridge Collapse Your Textbook Got Wrong
Galloping Gertie: The Bridge Your Textbook Got Wrong
description:
In the summer of 1940, the new Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State moved in the wind. Not a little. Its road rose and fell in waves you could see from the shore, and people came on purpose to drive across and feel it. The workers called it Galloping Gertie.

On 7 November 1940, just four months after it opened, a wind of around 40 miles an hour twisted the bridge until 600 feet of its deck fell into the water. No person died. The one death was a dog named Tubby.

The famous film of the collapse is in almost every physics class, usually with one word attached: resonance. That explanation is incomplete. This is the real story: the cheaper, slimmer design that replaced a safer one, the fixes that failed, the last morning, and the mechanism engineers call flutter.

Billah and R. H. Scanlan, American Journal of Physics (1991); Wikipedia, Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940).

AI note: narration voice and visuals are AI-generated; no images show the real people involved.
